artifacts.summary: Live reproduction of all three lean-challenge-snapshot.sh defects (declaration-chunk over-reach, ASCII-only identifier regex, Goals backtick over-read); corrects the dispatch's stale claims about already-landed source-store work (a third repair, R8, is already landed uncommitted, bringing the suite to 17 passed) and deploy-tree freshness (deployed copy is already byte-identical to the source store, missing only one fixture file).

memory_candidates.content: lean-challenge-snapshot.sh's declaration-boundary assemblers (extract_r1/extract_r2) compute each forced-sorry chunk as text[match[i].start():match[i+1].start()], then replace everything from the chunk's own first top-level ':=' through the chunk end with ' := sorry\n'. Any declaration keyword not in the matched alternation (e.g. abbrev, or an anonymous instance with no captured name) sitting inside that span is not a separate match, so its entire text is silently deleted rather than preserved or flagged. The same alternation and identifier-charset issues appear at multiple sites in a tool and must be fixed as one shared definition, not independently per site, or the sites end up disagreeing about what counts as a declaration.

An ASCII-only identifier regex applied to a backtick-delimited token (e.g. `` `([a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_']*)` ``) fails closed (no match at all) when the non-ASCII character is required to be immediately followed by the closing backtick, but the SAME regex applied to bare (non-delimited) source text truncates instead of failing, because nothing constrains what follows the captured run. This asymmetry means one ASCII-only regex can escape a cross-check entirely in one context and silently truncate-and-collide with an unrelated real identifier in another context, in the same tool, from the same root cause. Verified empirically with Python's default-Unicode re module: `\w` already matches Unicode letters and even subscript digits (category No) like U+2081, which is a better default continuation class than a hand-rolled `[A-Za-z0-9_]`.

When a dispatch's 'already-landed, uncommitted' section describes prior work in a source store, re-verify it empirically (run the test suite, diff deployed vs source-store files) rather than trusting the description as current -- a prior session can land further uncommitted work after the dispatch was generated, making the dispatch's landed-work description and its deploy-staleness claim both stale by the time research runs. In this case the actual suite had progressed from 16 to 17 passing cases and the deployed copy, which the dispatch claimed was stale, was already byte-identical to the source store.
